scope: Complete recursive Chapter12: envelopes and volumes of singularities
analytic_review_groups: Smooth exponential approximation fixes the smoothing index after the accuracy; the determinant lower bound need not be uniform in that index. Uniform convergence and bounded product continuity give smooth-obstacle contact.

Infimal convolution approximates a bounded lower-semicontinuous obstacle from below. Increasing bounded envelopes converge after regularization; zero mass on the strict open gap and bounded domination identify the limit.

Decreasing lower-semicontinuous approximation uses a fixed bounded quasi-continuous weight. Varying semipositive backgrounds are expanded with respect to one fixed Hermitian background before passing to the limit.

General contact first caps the obstacle above without changing its envelope. Two independent truncation levels and the weighted capacity convergence exhaust the strict gap even for infinite total extended mass.
The rooftop contact partition assigns the common contact to the second term. Ordered contact is used away from poles, and extended measures discard these pole sets.
An envelope fixed point equals the rooftop of its unit translate and zero. Its measure is bounded by the smooth measure on contact with zero; the translate-contact contributes only on poles.
Logarithmic growth delta corresponds to delta/2 times the Fubini–Study background. The projective representatives extend canonically across infinity, and the two maps are inverse.

Non-pluripolar compact-obstacle constraints give a common upper bound, while constants give a lower bound. Raw and regularized affine envelopes agree almost everywhere, not necessarily on the compact set.
A decreasing normalized projective series gives a logarithmic pole barrier on every pluripolar affine set. Convex repair of each competitor preserves the exact growth allowance.

The raw-contact parameters form a relatively closed upper ray. Pointwise concavity passes through almost-everywhere agreement to regularized envelopes; nonnegative concave defects give precisely the stated zero-set alternatives.

Independent competitors give the lower growth-increment bound; scaling gives the upper bound. Concavity yields finite initial slopes, and the obstacle sandwich gives the uniform oscillation-over-increment error at infinity.
At regular contact, vanishing growth derivative forces all later contact; a positive derivative makes the starting parameter the minimal raw-contact parameter.

Quasi-everywhere constraints admit the regularized envelope itself. Hahn–Banach supports the concave Lipschitz functional on C(K); positivity and constant translation identify a probability and a nonnegative penalty.
The fixed-growth supporting representation scales exactly in delta. Every penalty is at least the unweighted extremal value, and a minimizing support exists.
Bounded penalties give compact supporting-pair slices. Perturbed minimizing pairs converge to active pairs and recover the minimum penalty formula for the right growth derivative.

Joint weight and growth Lipschitz estimates use a positive lower bound for growth. Active pairs are convex and compact; weak convergence and uniform weight convergence preserve their defining equality.
Upper bounds from a fixed active pair and lower bounds from perturbed active pairs give the joint directional derivative and stability under convergence of directions.
Left and right growth derivatives are the maximum and minimum active penalty. Disjoint nonempty derivative-gap intervals contain distinct rationals, giving countably many corners.
Weight Gâteaux differentiability is equivalent to a single active probability; continuous test functions separate measures and the active equality fixes the penalty.

The quadratic disk example checks the circle derivative jump delta-2b is nonnegative. The two signs of the weight parameter give distinct derivatives without confusing raw and regularized constraints.
Local relative extremal functions vanish for pluripolar sets. A fixed logarithmic collar glues bounded local competitors to global ones and proves the exact unweighted zero-value criterion.
Upper-semicontinuity of the weight makes suprema on shrinking compact pieces tend to the point value. Raw contact is inherited by subsets and persists under larger growth allowances.
A locally strict global weight glues a local relative-extremal competitor by a maximum, giving the quantitative c*r^2 defect. Contact is equivalent to local pluriregularity in this regime.
Loss of later contact for a C2 plurisubharmonic weight forces its top Hessian power to vanish; positive definiteness would give a uniform strict local bound.
The planar weighted logarithm series converges through normalized projective potentials. Explicit disk distances give the negative barrier and its strictly positive value at the accumulation point.
The product compact has non-pluripolar pieces in every neighborhood. A hyperplane-pole correction repairs raw constraints; almost-everywhere order retains the regularization defect at the hyperplane.
A transverse complex line supplies circles lying in the compact set and proves the no-jump inequality at the distinguished point, without claiming local pluriregularity.
A strict big-background barrier and a bounded envelope in a Hermitian subbackground transfer positive individual mass by ordered contact. No positive uniform lower-mass bound is assumed.

Bounded semipositive domination uses contact support and positive individual mass to bound envelope suprema. A fixed strict sublevel has positive volume, contradicting normalized L1 compactness as the stretch grows.
Singularity-volume infima and suprema are unchanged by bounded potential changes and smooth gauge transport; positive scaling gives exactly t^n.
Relative competitors use convex combinations defined at common poles. Convexity, bounded changes, reference transport and smooth gauge transport preserve every finite stretch.
Composed stretches prove closure under stretching; averaging N finite stretches constructs a competitor for a finite rooftop. The countable translate example explains why finiteness is essential.
Relative members have the same singularity envelope for every smooth obstacle. Uniform normalized L1 bounds allow the convex coefficient to tend to one without a bounded-mass assumption.

A model reference with room in a smaller background and the relative difference envelope give smaller-background competitors for every member. Contact transfers a lower mass bound and positive individual mass, even when the uniform lower mass is zero.

Smooth finite heads and tails with arbitrarily small curvature loss provide every fixed finite stretch of the infinite-mass witness. The same construction works after positive scaling, with zero singularity envelope and trivial multiplier ideals.

The infinite-mass example distinguishes fixed-point finiteness from finiteness of all potentials sharing its envelope; it proves the stated bounded-mass equivalences without new general problem closures.
